Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, using the local distribution convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. For $p\in\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, call $(p,\xi)$ regular for $u$ if there are $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\chi=1$ near $p$ and an open cone $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ containing $\xi$ such that for every integer $N\ge0$,
$$ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}(1+|\eta|)^N\left|\left\langle u,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|\right\rangle\right|<\infty. $$
The local wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_\Omega(u)$ is the complement of these regular pairs in $T^*\Omega\setminus0$, with the standard cotangent coordinates $(p,\xi)$. A cone is invariant under multiplication by positive scalars. This is a chart-level definition; this item makes no assertion about its behavior under a change of coordinates.

Let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$, with signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. A cotangent vector is future or past causal when its metric dual belongs to the corresponding closed causal tangent cone. For $r\ge1$, let $\overline V_\pm^r\subset T^*M^r\setminus0$ consist of tuples $(x_1,\ldots,x_r;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r)$ such that every $\xi_j$ is either zero or future causal for $+$, respectively past causal for $-$, and the total tuple is nonzero. The wavefront set used below is the set of nonzero cotangent tuples where compactly localized Fourier transforms fail rapid decay in every conic neighborhood.

A compactly supported polynomial functional is a finite expression
$$ F(\phi)=\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left\langle f_m,\phi^{\otimes m}\mu_g^{\otimes m}\right\rangle, $$
where $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, $f_m\in\mathcal E'(M^m)$ is symmetric under permutations of its $m$ variables, $\mu_g$ is the metric density fixed by the Lorentzian metric, and the pairing is defined by inserting a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ in the smooth factor. Its $r$th functional derivative $F^{(r)}(\phi)\in\mathcal E'(M^r)$ is specified, for a test density $\omega$ on $M^r$, by
$$ \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi),\omega\right\rangle =\sum_{m=r}^{N}\frac{m!}{(m-r)!} \left\langle f_m,\omega\otimes\phi^{\otimes(m-r)}\mu_g^{\otimes(m-r)}\right\rangle, $$
where a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ is inserted in the smooth $\phi$ factors. Expanding the finite polynomial shows that this kernel represents the directional derivative in smooth compactly supported real directions. The functional is microcausal when
$$ \operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\cap(\overline V_+^r\cup\overline V_-^r)=\varnothing $$
for every $r\ge1$ and every $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$. Write $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$ for this class, including constants.

Let $M$ first be any Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary and $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$. No metric, orientation or dimension restriction is used in the following wavefront definition. For each smooth chart $x:U	o\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):= igcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are the local Fourier wavefront sets. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

derivations.claim: Expand the finite polynomial in the definition of $F$ after substituting $\phi+\sum_jt_jh_j$ and take the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_r$. Each resulting term is $\int a(x)\prod_{j=1}^{r}\partial^{\alpha_j}h_j(x)\,d^4x$, with $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M)$. Write $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$, $i(x)=(x,\ldots,x)$ and $A=\sum_j|\alpha_j|$. Its kernel is $u=(-1)^A\partial_{x_1}^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_{x_r}^{\alpha_r}[a(x_r)\prod_{j<r}\delta(x_j-x_r)]$: pairing it with a product test and using distributional differentiation gives the displayed integral. More generally its value on $v(X)|dX|$ is $\int a(x)(\partial_{x_1}^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_{x_r}^{\alpha_r}v)(i(x))\,d^4x$. Thus the complete kernel is a finite sum of finite derivatives of smooth compact diagonal distributions, supported on $\Delta_r$. This includes $r=1$, with the empty delta product equal to $1$, and gives the zero kernel above the finite polynomial degree. Derivatives of the relative deltas are retained; they cannot in general all be transferred to $a$.

Fix an arbitrary smooth ambient chart $\psi:O\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^{4r}$, a point $q=i(x_0)\in O$, and a nonzero chart covector $\eta_0$ with $D(\psi\circ i)(x_0)^T\eta_0\ne0$. Put $f=\psi\circ i$ on $i^{-1}(O)$. By continuity, there are a relatively compact neighborhood $B$ of $x_0$, an open cone $\mathcal C$ about $\eta_0$, and $c>0$ such that $|Df(x)^T\eta|\ge c|\eta|$ on $\overline B\times\mathcal C$. Indeed the left side divided by $|\eta|$ is continuous in $x$ and $\eta/|\eta|$ and positive at $(x_0,\eta_0/|\eta_0|)$; restrict to a small closed ball and a small closed spherical cap contained in that positive neighborhood. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(V)$ equal to one near $\psi(q)$, with $i^{-1}(\psi^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\chi))\subset B$. Such a localization is obtained by taking a sufficiently small chart ball inside $\psi(O\cap\{X:x_r\in B\})$. Smooth plateaus in nested balls follow explicitly from $H(t)=0$ for $t\le0$, $H(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$: for radii $0<b<R$, the ratio $H(R^2-|y-y_0|^2)/(H(R^2-|y-y_0|^2)+H(|y-y_0|^2-b^2))$ is one on the smaller ball and zero outside the larger, and is smooth because all derivatives of $H$ at zero vanish. No family of charts or localizations is selected. In the test-density convention underlying [F1]–[F2], put $J_\psi(X)=|\det D\psi(X)|$. For a summand $u$ from step 1.1 its chart Fourier pairing is
$$\langle u_\psi,\chi(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\eta}|dy|\rangle=\int a(x)\left.\partial_X^\alpha\!\left[J_\psi(X)\chi(\psi(X))e^{-2\pi i\eta\cdot\psi(X)}\right]\right|_{X=i(x)}d^4x.$$
Here $\partial_X^\alpha$ denotes the finite ambient derivative from step 1.1. The absolute Jacobian is smooth since the chart determinant never vanishes. Repeated product and chain rules make this a finite sum $\int A_\beta(x,\eta)e^{-2\pi i\eta\cdot f(x)}d^4x$, where each amplitude is a polynomial in $\eta$ of degree at most $m:=|\alpha|$, with smooth coefficients supported in one compact $K\subset B$. The coefficients include every derivative of the Jacobian, localization and chart map. Consequently, for every integer $k\ge0$, their derivatives satisfy $\max_{|\gamma|\le k}\sup_x|\partial_x^\gamma A_\beta(x,\eta)|\le C_k(1+|\eta|)^m$. This follows by bounding the finitely many coefficient derivatives on $K$; no bound on a varying test function is asserted.

For $\eta\in\mathcal C$, $|\eta|\ge1$, set $\Phi_\eta(x)=\eta\cdot f(x)$, $b_\eta=
abla\Phi_\eta/|
abla\Phi_\eta|^2$, and $L_\eta=-(2\pi i)^{-1}b_\eta\cdot
abla_x$. Then $L_\eta e^{-2\pi i\Phi_\eta}=e^{-2\pi i\Phi_\eta}$. Every derivative of $
abla\Phi_\eta$ is bounded by a constant times $|\eta|$ on $\overline B$, while its squared norm is at least $c^2|\eta|^2$. Differentiating the quotient therefore gives $\sup_{\overline B}|\partial_x^\gamma b_\eta|\le C_\gamma|\eta|^{-1}$: equivalently write $b_\eta=|\eta|^{-1}b_{\eta/|\eta|}$, and differentiate the smooth rational expression on the compact base ball and closed spherical cap where its denominator is bounded below. The transpose for the bilinear integral is $L_\eta^t A=(2\pi i)^{-1}\operatorname{div}(b_\eta A)$. Compact support of each amplitude eliminates boundary terms, so $N$ integrations by parts give
$$\int A_ eta e^{-2\pi i\Phi_\eta}\,dx=\int (L_\eta^t)^N A_ eta\,e^{-2\pi i\Phi_\eta}\,dx,\qquad \left|\int A_ eta e^{-2\pi i\Phi_\eta}\,dxight|\le C_N|\eta|^{m-N}.$$
For completeness, induction on $N$ expands $(L_\eta^t)^N A_ eta$ into finitely many terms, each a derivative of $A_ eta$ of order at most $N$ times $N$ factors that are derivatives of components of $b_\eta$ of orders at most $N$. The bounds of step 2.1 and the preceding quotient bounds give the estimate, and integration over a fixed rectangle containing $K$ supplies its finite volume factor. Integration by parts itself follows componentwise from the ordinary product rule and the fundamental theorem on that rectangle, with zero boundary products. For $|\eta|\le1$ the original finite polynomial amplitudes give a uniform integral bound directly. Given any requested decay power $p$, choose a finite integer $N\ge p+\max|\alpha|$ over the finitely many kernel terms; the finite sum of all kernel terms then has $(1+|\eta|)^p$ times its localized Fourier pairing bounded throughout $\mathcal C$.

If $q\notin\Delta_r$, a localization disjoint from the closed diagonal makes the kernel zero by step 1.1. At a diagonal point, steps 2.1–3.1 exclude every chart direction for which $Df(x_0)^T\eta\ne0$. The intrinsic covector represented by $\eta$ is $\xi=D\psi_q^T\eta$; the ordinary chain rule gives $Df(x_0)^T\eta=Di_{x_0}^T\xi=\sum_j\xi_j$. Thus, in every arbitrary ambient chart, the only possible singular directions annihilate the tangent to the diagonal. Taking the all-chart union in [F4]'s wavefront convention therefore proves precisely $\operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\subseteq N^*\Delta_r\setminus0$. No chart-invariance theorem is invoked. For $r=1$, $i$ is the identity and $D\psi$ is invertible, so every nonzero direction has been excluded and the wavefront set is empty.

At a diagonal point, if $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r$ are all future causal, their metric-dual time components have the same weak sign, and each nonzero causal covector has a strictly nonzero time component. Hence $\sum_j\xi_j=0$ forces every $\xi_j=0$; the same holds for the past cone. Step 4.1 therefore excludes every nonzero tuple in the forbidden cones of [F3]. The finite Taylor expansion of the original polynomial at $\phi=0$ gives its symmetric compact coefficient kernels $f_m=F^{(m)}(0)/m!$ (and its constant term), so it is also a polynomial functional in the kernel sense of [F3]. Its derivative kernels have the conormal bound just proved for every smooth $\phi$ and every $r\ge1$. This proves the asserted membership in $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. All localizations, finite expansions and integrations above were constructed for a fixed chart and direction; this proof adds no choice principle.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. When $x=y$, require $\xi=\zeta$ and allow every nonzero null covector. This relation is unsigned: the future first-covector condition below selects $\lambda>0$, while the Feynman past branch selects $\lambda<0$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. At the extension stage, numerical coefficients on independent balanced labels admit extensions across the total diagonal preserving their actual scaling degree; the final normalization conditions below are imposed within the engineering upper bounds. $$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. Any two extensions of a fixed punctured coefficient with upper bound $B_\Gamma$ differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, its actual degree replaces $B_\Gamma$ in this ambiguity bound. Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by

where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$

A surjective linear pullback does not increase that bound: in coordinates $(y,z)$ with $y=Lx$, $L^*T=T(y)\otimes1(z)$, and integration of a test in $z$ cancels the extra dilation Jacobian. The same observation shows that a translation-invariant kernel, written as a relative distribution tensored with a constant center coordinate, has the same full-coordinate and relative scaling bounds. Its wavefront covectors satisfy $\sum_i\xi_i=0$: with a product localization in center and relative coordinates the center Fourier transform decreases rapidly, and the convolution localization argument of [F3] gives the statement for arbitrary localizations. Thus every cross edge $\partial^{\alpha_e}W(x_i,x_j)$ has upper scaling bound $2+|\alpha_e|$, while every lower-order block kernel has covectors whose sum within its block is zero.

Fix a nontrivial partition $I\mid J$ of the vertices. The extended subgraph kernels $t_I$ and $t_J$ are distributions on their entire separate coordinate blocks, including their own total diagonals. Lift the two kernels to the full vertex-coordinate space by tensoring with the constant distribution in the other block. Step 1.1 preserves their finite nonnegative upper scaling bounds $b_I,b_J$. All factors are already defined at the center where [F4] is used. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. When $x=y$, require $\xi=\zeta$ and allow every nonzero null covector. This relation is unsigned: the future first-covector condition below selects $\lambda>0$, while the Feynman past branch selects $\lambda<0$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition is imposed compatibly with integration by parts in the local functionals. First write every local density in its unique balanced-jet representative, in which the derivative variables at a degree-$r$ vertex are the relative combinations $q_a=p_a-r^{-1}\sum_bp_b$. At the extension stage, numerical coefficients on independent balanced labels admit extensions across the total diagonal preserving their actual scaling degree; the final normalization conditions below are imposed within the engineering upper bounds. General jet labels are recovered by total coordinate differentiation of the already extended full coefficients and by linearity; this includes differentiation of the remaining field jets. For a primitive differentiated graph the required upper scaling bound is the engineering degree
$$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. Any two extensions of a fixed punctured coefficient with upper bound $B_\Gamma$ differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$. The allowed counterterms must also satisfy the stated linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, its actual degree replaces $B_\Gamma$ in this ambiguity bound. A differentiated coefficient is not required to retain the exact scaling degree of a punctured linear combination that vanishes: total differentiation may force a contact term at the diagonal.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

For every $F\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$, every $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ and every $r\ge1$, the kernel $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\subseteq N^*\Delta_r\setminus0,$$
where $\Delta_r=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and
$$N^*\Delta_r=\{(x,\ldots,x;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r):\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_r=0\}.$$
Consequently $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ avoids the all-future and all-past causal cotangent cones and $F$ belongs to $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $\hbar$ be a formal indeterminate. Let $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ be a scalar Hadamard bisolution. For $F,G\in\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$, let $\deg F$ be the largest degree with nonzero coefficient kernel, with $\deg 0=0$, and define, coefficientwise in $\hbar$,
$$ F\star_W G =\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)} \frac{\hbar^r}{r!} \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),\,W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle. $$
Each term is formed by the distribution product on the $r$ contracted variable pairs and proper pushforward over those pairs, as in [[thm-qftx-wavefront-product]], integrating with the metric density $\mu_g$ in each contracted variable. The sum is finite and defines a member of $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$. If $K\in C^\infty(M\times M)$ is symmetric, then
$$ \Gamma_KF(\phi)=\left\langle F^{(2)}(\phi),\chi K\mu_g^{\otimes2}\right\rangle $$
is also a compactly supported polynomial microcausal functional and lowers polynomial degree by two; here $\chi$ is any compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}F^{(2)}(\phi)$.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and fix admissible scalar free data as defined by the local time-ordered product contract. Fix a finite loopless multigraph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $n\ge2$, parallel edges allowed, and a finite multi-index derivative $\alpha_e$ on each edge $e$. In this lemma a vertex subgraph is always the induced multigraph $\Gamma[S]$ on a subset $S\subseteq V$: it retains all edges of $\Gamma$ whose two endpoints lie in $S$, with their multiplicities and derivative labels. The associated partial diagonal is $\Delta_S=\{(x_i)_{i\in V}\in(\mathbb R^4)^V:x_i=x_j\text{ for all }i,j\in S\}$; its codimension is $4(|S|-1)$, and $\Delta_V$ is the total diagonal. Put $i_0=\min S$ and use $(x_i-x_{i_0})_{i\in S\setminus\{i_0\}}$ as relative coordinates on the quotient by simultaneous translations. The scaling degree at $\Delta_S$ means the scaling degree at the origin in these relative coordinates, using positive dilations as in the scaling-degree definition. For $|S|\ge2$, let $t_{\Gamma[S]}$ be the numerical coefficient on the complement of its total diagonal after the coefficients for all strictly smaller vertex subsets $T\subsetneq S$, $|T|\ge2$, have been extended across their partial diagonals. Call $\Gamma[S]$ divergent exactly when $\operatorname{sd}_0(t_{\Gamma[S]})\ge4(|S|-1)$; call $\Gamma$ primitive when none of its proper induced vertex subgraphs is divergent. A translation-invariant extension here is invariant under simultaneous translations of all vertices in the relevant subset.

Suppose for every proper subset $S\subsetneq V$ with $|S|\ge2$, the coefficient $t_{\Gamma[S]}$ has already received a translation-invariant extension across its total diagonal, obeying the scaling upper bounds of the contract and agreeing on intersections, by induction on $|S|$. Then the numerical graph distribution $t_\Gamma$ on the complement of the total diagonal has a finite upper scaling bound in the $4(n-1)$ relative coordinates. For a primitive graph, the bound is
$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t_\Gamma)\le 2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_{e\in E(\Gamma)}|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph with proper subgraphs, the same induction gives a finite bound obtained from this edge estimate and the finitely many derivative orders of its lower-order local counterterms.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Thus the same-degree freedom is finite dimensional, with precisely the displayed delta derivatives as its basis; at the threshold $\delta=n$, only a multiple of $\delta_0$ is allowed.

Let $\mathfrak l$ be the six-dimensional real Lie algebra with basis $J_1,J_2,J_3,K_1,K_2,K_3$ and brackets $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_k$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, where $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. This fixes the convention for $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $\rho:\mathfrak l\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ be a real-linear representation, meaning $\rho([X,Y])=[\rho(X),\rho(Y)]$. If a real-linear map $c:\mathfrak l\to V$ satisfies the Lie-algebra $1$-cocycle identity

$$c([X,Y])=\rho(X)c(Y)-\rho(Y)c(X)\qquad(X,Y\in\mathfrak l),$$

then there is $v\in V$ such that $c(X)=\rho(X)v$ for every $X\in\mathfrak l$. No infinite-dimensional module, gauge cohomology, or interacting-field conclusion is asserted.

For $a\in\Omega$ and $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq\{a\}$ if and only if
$$u=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_a$$
for some finite $m\ge0$ and complex coefficients. The coefficients, with absent higher terms interpreted as zero, are unique. A nonzero such combination has support exactly $\{a\}$; the zero combination has empty support. This holds in ZF.

Assume Countable Choice. Set $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and let $SO^+(1,3)$ consist of the matrices $\Lambda\in GL_4(\mathbb R)$ satisfying $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preserving the future cone $\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|\mathbf v|\}$. For $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, let $\gamma$ be the affine map $x\mapsto\Lambda x+a$ and define
$$(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),\qquad (\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi).$$
Complex conjugation is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.

For field degree $r\ge1$, let $p_1,\ldots,p_r\in\mathbb R^4$ be formal commuting derivative variables, put $P=\sum_a p_a$ and $q_a=p_a-P/r$, and let $\mathcal B_r$ be the vector space of permutation-invariant polynomials in the $q_a$, subject to $\sum_aq_a=0$. A balanced degree-$r$ jet polynomial is
$$B_b(\phi)(x)=\left.b(\partial_{x_1},\ldots,\partial_{x_r})\prod_{a=1}^r\phi(x_a)\right|_{x_1=\cdots=x_r=x},\qquad b\in\mathcal B_r.$$
Thus only relative derivative combinations occur in $b$. Choose a real homogeneous basis of each finite-degree part of $\mathcal B_r$. Every off-shell compactly supported local polynomial functional has a unique expression
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{r\ge1}\sum_b\int f_{r,b}(x)B_b(\phi)(x)\,d^4x,$$
with $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_{r,b}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$, and only finitely many nonzero coefficients. The union of the supports of these coefficient functions equals the functional support, apart from the constant $c$, whose support is empty. With each $p_a$ viewed as a column of coordinate derivative components, the induced Lorentz substitution is $p_a\mapsto\Lambda^{\mathsf T}p_a$, so $P$ and all $q_a$ transform by the same linear map. The balanced decomposition is equivariant for the translation/Lorentz action and complex conjugation specified above.

Distribution-valued multilinear coefficients prescribed linearly on balanced labels extend consistently to all polynomial jet labels by imposing, in each vertex entry,
$$K(\ldots,\partial_\mu A,\ldots)=\partial_{x_i^\mu}K(\ldots,A,\ldots).$$
After smearing, integration by parts therefore makes the resulting maps independent of the chosen local density presentation. Differentiation adds only a finite derivative order to any finite scaling upper bound.

For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, the space $\mathcal D_K$ is Hausdorff, locally convex and complete for
$$d(f,g)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(f-g)).$$
This metric induces exactly its derivative-seminorm topology. Multiplying the metric by two gives the equivalent convention with weights $2^{-m}$. These assertions require no choice axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ($\mathrm{DC}$). If a nonempty metric space $X$ is complete, then it is not the union of a sequence of closed sets each having empty interior. Equivalently, the intersection of countably many open dense subsets of $X$ is dense.

derivations.claim: Set $T_0=1$ and $T_1=\operatorname{id}$, as required. Use the unique balanced representative [F11] in every positive field-degree entry; a constant entry is interpreted as the corresponding scalar times the lower multilinear map, consistently with its empty functional support. Perform the extension construction below first on balanced labels. For total derivatives of those labels use the derivative identity in [F11], with derivatives acting on the full coefficient, including its remaining field jets. This guarantees that the resulting multilinear maps depend only on the actual local functionals and respect integration by parts, before any extension choices are made. Assume $T_k$ has been constructed with all contract properties for every $k<n$, where $n\ge2$.

In $\mathbb M^n$ let $\Delta_n=\{x_1=\cdots=x_n\}$. For every nonempty proper $I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ define
$$C_I=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i
otin J^-(x_j)	ext{ for all }i\in I,\ j
otin I\}.$$
Each $C_I$ is open because the Minkowski causal relation is closed. To see these sets cover $\mathbb M^n\setminus\Delta_n$, choose two distinct coordinates $p,q$ in a configuration. The open cone of past-timelike covectors cannot annihilate the nonzero displacement $p-q$, so choose a past-timelike covector $	au$ with $	au(p)
e	au(q)$. Choose $s$ strictly between these values and different from the finitely many $	au(x_j)$, and put $I=\{j:	au(x_j)>s\}$. The hyperplane $	au(x)=s$ is spacelike, and $	au$ is strictly increasing on every future causal curve. Thus no $x_i$ with $i\in I$ can lie in $J^-(x_j)$ for $j
otin I$, so the configuration lies in $C_I$.

Expand the finite local polynomial derivatives in the graph convention of [F1]. For each fixed $n$, finite jet order and finite polynomial degree allow only finitely many labeled multigraphs, and every edge derivative order is finite. By [F6], after the already constructed proper subgraph extensions, each numerical coefficient $t_\Gamma$ on the punctured relative space $\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}\setminus\{0\}$ has a finite upper scaling bound and scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma<+\infty$.

On $C_I$, define the lower-order product $T^I_n=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_WT_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$. The factors are microcausal by [F2] and the inductive hypothesis, so [F3] makes the product well-defined; each contraction in its finite graph expansion uses only the pullbacks and distribution products supplied by [F4]. The graph-kernel restriction on this stratum is therefore a distribution, and no separate product at the total diagonal is taken here.

If $C_I$ and $C_J$ overlap, put $A=I\cap J$, $B=I\setminus J$, $C=J\setminus I$, and $D=(I\cup J)^c$. The defining inequalities give $A$ later than or spacelike to $B$, $C$ later than or spacelike to $D$, $A$ later than or spacelike to $C$, and $B$ later than or spacelike to $D$. They also imply that every point of $B$ is spacelike to every point of $C$: neither causal ordering is possible. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. When $x=y$, require $\xi=\zeta$ and allow every nonzero null covector. This relation is unsigned: the future first-covector condition below selects $\lambda>0$, while the Feynman past branch selects $\lambda<0$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. One has interior, so subtracting two elements of that interior and rescaling gives $|L_\rho(\varphi)|\le C p_m(\varphi)$ uniformly in $\rho$, with $p_m=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\varphi\|_\infty$. The same argument then applies to $v$ and to every fixed compact scale interval.

Choose slightly enlarged closed frequency cones $K_j$ around the $C_j$ such that the joint no-cancellation condition still holds for the $K_j$. This is possible by compactness of tuples with $\sum_j|\xi_j|=1$: the set of tuples in $\prod_j(C_j\cup\{0\})$ is compact there and its sum stays away from zero. If $C_j$ is empty use the empty cone. Closedness of the wavefront set permits localization to a sufficiently small common neighborhood so that all singular directions of each localized $v_j$ lie strictly inside $K_j$. Choose a smooth Fourier cutoff $q_j$ supported in $K_j$ outside a bounded ball and equal to one around those singular directions at large frequencies. Then $(1-q_j)\widehat v_j$ is Schwartz. In fact [F3] gives rapid decay on its unbounded support, while each frequency derivative is a localized Fourier transform with a coordinate monomial inserted, so has the same regular-cone bounds by [F3]–[F4]. Bounded frequencies cause no problem. Thus $v_j=b_j+c_j$, with $b_j$ Schwartz and the Fourier transform of $c_j$ supported in $K_j$ together with a bounded ball.

The family $L_\rho=\rho^s v_\rho$ is uniformly bounded on Schwartz space by one Schwartz seminorm. Indeed, decompose a Schwartz test into a fixed ball and smooth dyadic annuli of radii $R=2^k\ge1$. On an annulus write $\varphi_R(x)=\theta(x/R)\varphi(x)$ with one fixed annular cutoff. Dilation gives
$$\langle\rho^s v_\rho,\varphi_R\rangle=R^{D-s}\langle(\rho R)^s v_{\rho R},\theta(y)\varphi(Ry)\rangle.$$
If $\operatorname{supp}v\subset B(0,M)$, annuli with $\rho R>2M$ give zero, after increasing $M$ to accommodate the fixed annular radii. For $0<\rho R\le2M$, step 1.1 on the one fixed annulus bounds this by $C R^{D-s+m-L}P_{m,L}(\varphi)$, where $P_{m,L}(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_x(1+|x|)^L|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|$. Choose $L>D-s+m+1$; the geometric sum over $R=2^k$ is finite uniformly in $\rho$. The fixed ball is controlled by step 1.1. This proves $|\langle L_\rho,\varphi\rangle|\le C'P_{m',L'}(\varphi)$ for fixed $m',L',C'$ independent of $\rho$. By transposition [F5] the Fourier transforms are likewise uniformly tempered.

For $s_j>a_j\ge0$, step 2.1 makes $\rho^{s_j}(v_j)_\rho$ uniformly tempered. The Schwartz part $\rho^{s_j}(b_j)_\rho$ is also uniformly tempered, since $b_j(\rho x)$ and each of its derivatives are bounded uniformly for $0<\rho\le1$, and its local smooth seminorms tend to zero. Consequently the Fourier family of $\rho^{s_j}(c_j)_\rho$ is uniformly tempered and supported in $K_j$ together with a fixed bounded ball: dilation shrinks that ball in frequency. Let $V$ be a closed cone disjoint from a slightly larger cone around $K_j$, and let $\chi$ be any fixed compact smooth test cutoff. Evaluate the localized Fourier transform by pairing this Fourier family with $\widehat\chi(\xi-\eta)$ times a smooth cutoff equal to one on its support. On the unbounded conic support, separation gives $|\xi-\eta|\ge c(|\xi|+|\eta|)$ for $\xi\in V$; on the bounded part use $1+|\xi-\eta|\ge c'(1+|\xi|)$ for large $\xi$. Every Schwartz seminorm of this test kernel is therefore $O((1+|\xi|)^{-N})$ for arbitrary $N$. The uniform tempered bound gives
$$\sup_{0<\rho\le1}\sup_{\xi\in V}(1+|\xi|)^N\left|\widehat{\chi\rho^{s_j}(v_j)_\rho}(\xi)\right|<\infty.$$
The Schwartz part has the same estimate by integration by parts on the fixed support of $\chi$. An intermediate exponent between $a_j$ and $s_j$ even makes each displayed seminorm tend to zero. Ordinary weak convergence follows from [F1]. Since $v_j=u_j$ near zero, every fixed output localization uses these same dilates for all sufficiently small $\rho$. This proves the required directional control rather than inferring it from pointwise wavefront inclusion of the rescaled family.

Shrink the cones and localization neighborhoods as in step 1.2, retaining a little angular margin. The product exists there by [F3], iterated over the finitely many factors. For a fixed compactly supported test $\varphi$, its pairing with the product of the localized scaled factors is the absolutely convergent Fourier integral of $\widehat\varphi(-\sum_j\eta_j)$ times the factor transforms. Here is a uniform integrable bound. Compactness of normalized frequency tuples and the joint no-cancellation condition imply that either $|\sum_j\eta_j|\ge c\sum_j|\eta_j|$, or some $\eta_j$ lies in a regular cone and $|\eta_j|\ge c\sum_k|\eta_k|$, for a fixed $c>0$, apart from bounded frequencies. In the first region the Schwartz decay of $\widehat\varphi$ controls the total frequency size; in the second region step 3.1 supplies arbitrarily high decay from that factor. All other localized factor transforms have fixed uniform polynomial bounds by step 1.1 and [F4]. Choosing the decay power larger than the total polynomial degree plus $Dr+1$ gives an integrable majorant independent of $\rho$. Each localized factor transform tends pointwise to zero by weak convergence. Dominated convergence therefore proves $\rho^{\sum_j s_j}\prod_j(u_j)_\rho\to0$. Dilation commutes with the locally defined product by the pullback formula [F3], so this is precisely the scaling estimate for the product. Let every $s_j$ decrease to $a_j$ to obtain the claimed bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Polarize each homogeneous field-degree-$r$ jet polynomial into $r$ field slots. Commutativity of the scalar fields identifies it with a polynomial in the formal derivative variables $p_a$, invariant under slot permutations. The invertible linear change $p_a=q_a+P/r$ identifies the full polynomial algebra with $\mathbb C[P]\otimes\mathbb C[q_1,\ldots,q_r]/(\sum_aq_a)$. Slot permutations fix $P$ and act only on the relative factor. Expanding in the independent monomials of $P$, invariance holds if and only if every relative coefficient is invariant. Thus the invariant space is exactly $\mathbb C[P]\otimes\mathcal B_r$. In each finite degree choose a basis by ordinary finite Gaussian elimination on the real coefficient polynomials; the monomial ordering gives compatible choices across degrees. The Leibniz rule identifies multiplication by $P_\mu$ with the total derivative $\partial_\mu$ of the local field polynomial. This is a direct tensor decomposition, so has no hidden relations between total and balanced derivatives.

Expand a density using step 1.1 as a finite sum $p(\partial)B_b$. In its integral against $f$, move $p(\partial)$ onto the compact coefficient by integration by parts, obtaining $p(-\partial)f$ multiplying $B_b$. This gives existence of the displayed representation and preserves compact support. Degree zero gives the scalar $c=F(0)$ and is separated from the positive field degrees. To prove uniqueness, suppose a balanced expression represents zero. Separate its field degrees by replacing $\phi$ by $t\phi$, polarize, and evaluate its $r$ slots on the smooth exponential fields $e^{2\pi i k_a\cdot x}$; complex exponentials are permitted by complex multilinear extension from real configurations. The resulting identity is a finite sum of $\widehat f_{r,b}(-\sum_a k_a)$ times the balanced polynomial $b(2\pi ik_1,\ldots,2\pi ik_r)$. For fixed total momentum, vary freely the relative momenta. Independence of the basis polynomials on $\sum_aq_a=0$ makes every coefficient Fourier transform zero at that total momentum. Since that momentum is arbitrary, [F2] gives every $f_{r,b}=0$; also $c=0$.

The same uniqueness is local. In center and relative coordinates for the polarized variational kernel on the thin diagonal, balanced differential operators differentiate only the relative delta variables; their coefficients are the $f_{r,b}$ in the center variable, up to fixed nonzero coordinate constants. Test with a center test times a relative monomial times a cutoff equal to one near the relative origin. Starting at the highest relative order and descending isolates every independent relative delta-jet coefficient. Thus vanishing of the kernel over an open center set forces each $f_{r,b}$ to vanish there. If $F$ is unchanged by all variations supported in an open set $U$, its polarized kernels vanish where any one field slot lies in $U$; near their thin diagonal this is precisely the preceding situation. Conversely, if every coefficient vanishes on $U$, no variation supported in $U$ changes $F$. This proves equality with the functional support. Under the action defined in the Statement, a Lorentz transformation substitutes $p_a\mapsto\Lambda^{\mathsf T}p_a$ and transforms each coefficient by $f(x)\mapsto f(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$; $\det\Lambda=1$ preserves $d^4x$. Thus $P$ and all $q_a$ transform by the same linear map and the tensor decomposition is preserved. Translations act on coefficients by the same formula with $\Lambda=I$, and, because the chosen basis is real, complex conjugation sends each coefficient to its complex conjugate. Hence the decomposition is equivariant as stated.

For a general polynomial label write its unique tensor decomposition as $\sum_{\beta,b}c_{\beta,b}\partial^\beta B_b$, and define its coefficient by $\sum_{\beta,b}c_{\beta,b}\partial_{x_i}^\beta K(\ldots,B_b,\ldots)$, independently in every entry. Commutativity of coordinate derivatives and the direct decomposition in step 1.1 make this consistent, linear, and the unique extension satisfying the displayed derivative identity. Smearing and integrating by parts gives exactly the coefficient normal form of step 2.1, so equivalent functional presentations yield the same map. The construction respects the equivariance and support statements of step 3.1. Finally, dilation of a distributional derivative gives $(\partial^\beta T)_\rho=\rho^{-|\beta|}\partial^\beta T_\rho$, so the added derivative increases a scaling upper bound by at most $|\beta|$. All sums and derivative orders here are finite.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. $$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
