No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition is imposed compatibly with integration by parts in the local functionals. First write every local density in its unique balanced-jet representative, in which the derivative variables at a degree-$r$ vertex are the relative combinations $q_a=p_a-r^{-1}\sum_bp_b$. At the extension stage, numerical coefficients on independent balanced labels admit extensions across the total diagonal preserving their actual scaling degree; the final normalization conditions below are imposed within the engineering upper bounds. General jet labels are recovered by total coordinate differentiation of the already extended full coefficients and by linearity; this includes differentiation of the remaining field jets. For a primitive differentiated graph the required upper scaling bound is the engineering degree
$$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. $$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{r\ge1}\sum_b\int f_{r,b}(x)B_b(\phi)(x)\,d^4x,$$
with $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_{r,b}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$, and only finitely many nonzero coefficients. With each $p_a$ viewed as a column of coordinate derivative components, the induced Lorentz substitution is $p_a\mapsto\Lambda^{\mathsf T}p_a$, so $P$ and all $q_a$ transform by the same linear map. Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. For $a\in\Omega$ and $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq\{a\}$ if and only if

$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$

$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

For a distribution $u$ on a smooth manifold, the chartwise rapid-decay definition of its wavefront set is independent of the chart: if $y=\psi(x)$, its covector coordinates satisfy $\eta=(D\psi(x))^{-T}\xi$. For distributions $u,v$ and a smooth diffeomorphism $\psi$, one has $\operatorname{WF}(u+v)\subseteq\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup\operatorname{WF}(v)$ and $\operatorname{WF}(\psi^*u)=\psi^*\operatorname{WF}(u)$. Finally, $\operatorname{WF}(u)=\varnothing$ exactly when $u$ is represented by a smooth scalar function in every chart.

$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Define the positive-frequency massless distribution by
$$w(t,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{e^{-i|\mathbf k|t+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}}{2|\mathbf k|(2\pi)^3}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
This is a distribution: pairing a compact smooth spacetime test gives its rapidly decreasing Fourier transform on the null mass shell, and $|\mathbf k|^{-1}d^3\mathbf k$ is integrable at zero and has polynomial growth at infinity. The mass-shell relation gives $Pw=0$. The measure is the restriction of $\theta(k^0)\delta((k^0)^2-|\mathbf k|^2)d^4k$, hence is invariant under the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; its reflection gives $w^*=w(-t,-\mathbf x)$. Scaling $\mathbf k$ shows that $w$ is nonzero homogeneous of degree $-2$. With a damping factor $e^{-\epsilon|\mathbf k|}$, angular integration and the elementary Laplace integral give
$$w_\epsilon(t,\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{4\pi^2}\frac{1}{|\mathbf x|^2-(t-i\epsilon)^2}.$$
The damped spectral integrals converge to $w$ on tests by the preceding absolute Fourier bound.

Define the time-ordered distribution by its spatial Fourier representation
$$h_F(t,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{e^{-i|\mathbf k||t|+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}}{2|\mathbf k|(2\pi)^3}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
